DEMONSTRATION DATA - NOT A REAL SYSTEM
This report was produced inside an isolated test environment (a Linux namespace with a root filesystem built only for this test). Every credential, file, permission and value shown here was deliberately planted with invented values. Nothing in this report comes from any real host, container, cloud account or network. See PROVENANCE.md for the per-finding breakdown of what was measured vs. what was planted.

high Docker socket present; Unix permissions would allow the workload to connect (estimate, untested)
INFRA-DOCKER-SOCKET-001 · mutation-potential
confirmed: Docker socket at /var/run/docker.sock (socket, mode 0666, readable by all users)
workload_user: uid 65534
Not verified: Actual connectability (no connection attempted), whether a daemon is listening, and whether its API authorizes the connection.
 Confirmed: the socket exists, and its Unix permission bits combined with the workload's UID suggest the workload could connect (root ignores file permission bits; a world-writable socket accepts any local user). This is a permission-model estimate only: user namespaces, MAC/LSM policies, or the absence of a listening daemon can all change the real outcome, and no connection was attempted. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if a Docker daemon answers on the other end, code in the container could control it - starting privileged containers, mounting host filesystems, reading other containers' data. Never mount /var/run/docker.sock into workloads. If a build needs it, use rootless builders or a constrained API proxy, and treat any container with socket access as trusted host-level code.
Verify: From outside the container, check the container spec for the socket mount and whether the workload genuinely needs it.
high AWS credential sources present (contents and validity unverified)
AWS-IDENTITY-001 · aws-identity
confirmed: AWS credentials file present on disk
workload_user: uid 65534
real_secret_values_exposed: false
Values (live run: real; secret values never collected): AWS_REGION = il-central-1
Not verified: Whether the files/provider actually yield valid credentials, which identity they represent, and what that identity is allowed to do - none of this is visible from inside the container.
 Confirmed: credential sources exist in places the workload can reach (a root workload can read any of them). Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they hold valid credentials, code running in the container could act as that AWS identity. Scope the task/instance role to the minimum required actions and resources, prefer the container credential provider over files on disk, and confirm actual permissions externally.
Verify: Authorized external check: IAM for the task/instance role, plus CloudTrail for its actual use.

Not verified: Allowlisted files (.env, AWS config/credentials) are parsed in memory with secret values masked before storage; private keys and tokens are never opened. Which masked fields hold live secrets, and why the files are readable by all users.
 Confirmed: files at conventional secret locations carry group/other read bits. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they contain real credentials, any process or user in the container - including untrusted code pulled from Git - could read them. A world-readable AWS config file may be benign; only its permissions are confirmed. Restrict to 0600 or tighter, chown to the runtime user, and remove credential files from images in favor of runtime secret injection.
Verify: Have the image owner confirm what these files contain and why they are world-readable.

 Confirmed: variable names matching secret patterns exist in the process environment; values were not read. Possible consequence, not confirmed here: if they hold live secrets, every process in the container can read them and they commonly leak into logs, crash reports, and child processes. Prefer mounted secret files with tight permissions or a secrets manager over environment variables; rotate anything that must stay in the environment.

Recommended next steps

  • Container-internal evidence cannot show what the available AWS role allows. Run a separate authorized external review (read-only audit account over IAM, VPC, and CloudTrail) before treating cloud permissions as known.
  • Treat tool and socket presence as leads, not proof: validate actual change permissions from outside the container before prioritizing remediation.
  • Address critical and high findings before running untrusted Git-sourced code in this container.
  • Untrusted code running in the same container can read or tamper with this report. In sensitive environments, treat the report as a local lead and verify externally.
Scope and limits. This report is read-only: it changes no settings and sends nothing externally. Credential, token, password, and private-key values are never retained or exported: secret-looking variables are never read, private keys are never opened, allowlisted files are parsed in memory with secret values masked before anything is written to the report. Secret material appears by name, path, and permission bits only. It cannot see full IAM permissions from inside a container, and a container does not necessarily see host processes, interfaces, or connections. Untrusted code sharing this container could read or tamper with this report; sensitive environments need a separate authorized external AWS/IAM/VPC/CloudTrail review. In fixture mode, any sample values or file contents shown are SYNTHETIC and invented for the demo - they are not real secrets and were not read from any real environment.
